match.reason: No point in the bank covers time lags in policy; the nearest ones, government failure, monetary policy, fiscal policy and conflicts between objectives, are related but teach different ideas.

draft.title: Time lags in policy
card: Recognition lag
the time it takes to see that a problem exists. Data such as unemployment or GDP is published after the period it describes, so a problem may be well under way before it is clear.
Decision lag
the time it takes to choose and approve a response. A fiscal measure may need a budget or a vote in Parliament, so it can take longer to decide than a change to the cash rate.
Impact lag
the time it takes for the policy to affect spending, jobs and prices. A change in interest rates can take many months to flow through to households and firms.
Because of these lags, the economy may have changed by the time a policy works. Policy can then arrive too late, or push too strongly on an economy that is already recovering.
draft.remember: Lags mean a policy can start working after the problem has already changed.

a.q: Why can time lags make a policy less effective?
opts: The economy may change before the policy takes effect
Households ignore any policy the government announces
Policies can only be used once the economy has recovered
Lags raise the cost of each policy to the government
a.why: Recognising, deciding and waiting for effects all take time, so conditions may be different when the policy finally works. The other options say things that the card does not support, such as households ignoring policy.
a.clue: Think about what happens to the economy while the policy is still on its way.

b.q: Unemployment in Australia rises for several months before official data shows it. The government then waits for a budget to approve extra spending. What does this describe?
opts: A recognition lag followed by a decision lag
A decision lag followed by an impact lag
An impact lag followed by a recognition lag
A recognition lag followed by an impact lag
b.why: Waiting for data to show the problem is a recognition lag. Waiting for the budget to approve spending is a decision lag. The impact lag comes later, when the spending starts to change jobs, so it is the tempting wrong answer here.
b.clue: Sort the two waits in the order they happen, before any money is spent.

a.best: The economy may change before the policy takes effect

b.best: A recognition lag followed by a decision lag

problems.detail: The clue says to sort the waits 'before any money is spent'. That rules out every option that mentions an impact lag, and all three wrong options do. A student can reach the answer from the clue alone, without telling a recognition lag from a decision lag.
